content: Meckel syndrome, type 1 (MKS1), is a protein in humans encoded by the MKS1 gene. The MKS1 protein, along with another protein called meckelin, is a component of the basal body proteome of the flagellar apparatus. These proteins are essential for the formation of cilia, which are hair-like structures on the surface of cells that play critical roles in cellular signaling and movement. Mutations in the MKS1 gene have been linked to the development of Meckel syndrome, a severe congenital disorder, as well as Bardet-Biedl syndrome, a condition characterized by a range of symptoms including retinal degeneration, obesity, and polydactyly. To study the function of MKS1, researchers have utilized model organisms. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Mks1tm1a(EUCOMM)Wtsi, was created as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This program is a large-scale mutagenesis initiative aimed at generating and distributing animal models of human diseases to the scientific community. Both male and female mice from this knockout line underwent a standardized series of phenotypic tests to assess the effects of the MKS1 gene deletion. A total of 25 tests were conducted on the mutant mice. In homozygous mutant embryos, significant abnormalities were observed, including polydactyly (extra digits), edema (swelling due to fluid accumulation), and defects in the eyes or craniofacial structures. These embryos did not survive to the weaning stage. In contrast, the remaining tests were performed on heterozygous mutant adult mice, and no additional abnormalities were detected in these animals.
